pages.name: Fifty readings
pages.text: Fifty readings have piled up round 115.0 V. A smooth curve follows the pile's outline: a bell. Most beads land near the middle and fewer land further out. A bead lands far out only when most of its twelve nudges push the same way. The smooth curve is the [[normal curve]], a model of such a pile. Some stacks stand above it and some below, because real counts wobble.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings of a UPS output fall from a hopper over 115.0 volts through a field of pegs and pile up on a beam balanced at their mean. A smooth curve traces the tops of the stacks, then relaxes into a bell.

pages.name: How often far out
pages.task: Landing 0.9 V high is 3 SD out. A bead needs most of its twelve nudges to push the same way. How often does that happen?
pages.answer: Rarely, as most mixes of nudges partly cancel
pages.why: Each nudge is as likely to push one way as the other. Most mixes of twelve partly cancel, so most beads land near the middle. To land far out, most of them must push the same way. That happens, but rarely. The path now drawn is the farthest bead's. It drifts the same way row after row.
pages.alt: The pile of fifty simulated readings under the peg field, with the bell-shaped normal curve over it. Few beads reach the ends. The path of the farthest bead through the pegs is drawn. It drifts the same way row after row.
options: Rarely, as most mixes of nudges partly cancel
About as often as landing near the middle
Never, as the nudges always cancel

pages.name: The bands
pages.text: The bands mark 1, 2 and 3 SD either side of the mean, and the tiles count the beads inside each. About 68% of readings sit within 1 SD of the mean. About 95% sit within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. A share of the time is a chance. So one honest reading has about a 95% chance of landing within 2 SD. That chance is its [[probability]], 0.95 written as a number from 0 to 1. The counts come close to what the curve expects.
pages.alt: The pile under its normal curve, with shaded bands 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations either side of the mean, bracketed above as 68, 95 and 99.7%.

pages.name: Beyond 2 SD
pages.task: Fifty honest readings pile into a bell. About how many do you expect beyond 2 SD of the mean?
pages.why: About 95% of honest readings land within 2 SD of the mean, so about 5% land beyond. And 5% of 50 is 2.5, so expect about 2 or 3. Here two land beyond the band, and each sends out a ring.
pages.alt: The pile of fifty simulated readings under its normal curve. A shaded band 2 standard deviations either side of the mean is bracketed 95%, and the two beads beyond it send out rings.

pages.name: The ruler
pages.text: To count a reading's distance from the mean, subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation. That count is the reading's [[z-score]]. The ruler over the pile is marked in z-scores. Its zero is the mean of the other forty-nine readings. Each mark is one of their standard deviations. The ringed reading is left out of both. A far-out reading would pull the mean towards it and widen the SD. That would shrink its own count. Here the ringed reading has slipped 0.6 V high, about 2 SD along the ruler.

pages.name: Count the SDs
pages.task: Readings of the UPS output have a mean of 115.0 V and a standard deviation of 0.3 V. One reads 116.0 V. How many SDs from the mean is it?
pages.why: Subtract the mean: 116.0 − 115.0 = 1.0 V. Then divide by the SD: 1.0 ÷ 0.3 is about 3.3. So it sits about 3.3 SD above the mean, far out on the ruler.

pages.name: One lands out
pages.task: Example limits sit 2 SD either side of the mean. You take fifty readings on rounds and one lands out. What does that show?
pages.answer: Little on its own, as honest readings land beyond 2 SD about one time in twenty
pages.why: About 95% of honest readings land within 2 SD, so about one in twenty lands beyond. In fifty readings, expect 2 or 3 out. So one out is chance at work, and it shows little on its own.
pages.alt: The pile under its normal curve with dashed example limits 2 standard deviations either side of the mean. One reading past the upper limit is marked as a warning. The band holding 95% fills the space between the limits.
options: Little on its own, as honest readings land beyond 2 SD about one time in twenty

pages.name: Far out on the ruler
pages.text: The ringed reading has slipped 1.2 V high, past the upper limit and about 4 SD out on the ruler. About 99.7% of honest readings land within 3 SD. So one this far out is more likely a slip or a real change. One common choice calls anything beyond about 3.3 SD an [[outlier]]. Yet honest readings do reach about 3 SD now and then. The other reading past the upper limit is honest, and about 3 SD out. So ask why before you delete it. Test again and look for a cause.

pages.name: What do you do
pages.task: On rounds the UPS output reads 116.2 V. Past readings have a mean of 115.0 V and a standard deviation of 0.3 V. What do you do?
pages.answer: Test again and look for a cause before deciding
pages.why: 116.2 − 115.0 = 1.2 V, and 1.2 ÷ 0.3 is 4 SD. Honest readings almost never land that far out. So it is more likely a slip, like a loose lead, or a real change. Test again and look for a cause. Then decide.

pages.name: Fresh batches
pages.text: Here is a fresh batch with its counts. The band counts wobble from batch to batch round what the curve expects. The ruler's marks shift a little as each batch's mean and SD change. The rule is an average over many batches, not a promise for each one. It also needs a bell. Some piles lean into a long tail, like the insulation resistance readings you met earlier. Then the far readings sit mostly on the long side.
pages.alt: A pile under its normal curve with its 1, 2 and 3 standard deviation bands, and the ruler in standard deviations above it.

pages.name: Above 115.6 V
pages.task: The UPS output has a mean of 115.0 V and a standard deviation of 0.3 V. An example upper limit sits at 115.6 V. About what share of honest readings land above it?
pages.why: 115.6 − 115.0 = 0.6 V, which is 2 SD. About 5% of honest readings land beyond 2 SD, half on each side, because the bell is symmetric. So about 2.5% land above 115.6 V. That is about one time in forty.
pages.alt: The pile under its normal curve with a dashed example upper limit at 115.6 volts. The band holding 95% ends at the limit, and the one reading above it is marked as a warning.

pages.name: A long tail
pages.task: Fifty insulation resistance readings lean into a long high tail. About what share land more than 2 SD above their mean?
pages.answer: More than the bell's 2.5%, out in the long tail
pages.why: The 2.5% comes from the bell, which is the same on both sides. This pile leans. Its far readings sit out in the long high tail. Here 2 of the 50 land more than 2 SD above the mean. That is 4%. None land that far below. So a far-high reading is much less rare than the bell says. Check the shape before you lean on the bell's shares.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated insulation resistance readings on an even scale of megohms. The pile leans, with a long tail of high readings, and the beam balances at their mean. A normal curve with the pile's own mean and standard deviation traces over it and does not fit. A band 2 standard deviations either side of the mean is shaded. The two readings beyond it send out rings, and both sit on the high side.
options: More than the bell's 2.5%, out in the long tail
About 2.5%, half of the 5% beyond 2 SD
Less than 2.5%, as most readings sit low
